one_liner: Header-only C++20 fixed-width uint128-uint512 integers for EVM and crypto code; no published win over GMP yet.
what_it_does: Provides allocation-free unsigned integer types uint<N> (N a multiple of 64, at least 128; aliases uint128 through uint512 and literals like 1_u256) stored as arrays of uint64_t words, with the full set of built-in-style operators, wrapping semantics and constexpr support including division. Extra helpers cover what the Ethereum VM needs: udivrem/sdivrem, addmod, mulmod, exp, clz/ctz/bit_width, bswap, and little- and big-endian load/store to byte arrays and spans. It is a value type replacement for hand-rolled 256-bit arithmetic, not a drop-in for GMP's mpz/mpn API.
how_it_is_fast: Everything is inline templates over a fixed word count, so there is no heap allocation, no size field and no dispatch; carries use compiler builtins (__builtin_addcll/__builtin_subcll or the x86 addcarryx/sbb intrinsics) and 64x64->128 products use unsigned __int128 or MSVC _umul128. Division follows Moller and Granlund's 'Improved division by invariant integers' (a table-seeded reciprocal_2by1/reciprocal_3by2 replaces the hardware divide), with dedicated 1-word and 2-word divisor paths and Knuth Algorithm D for longer divisors. addmod has a fast path for moduli of at least 2^192 with already-reduced operands (ported from holiman/uint256 PR #86).
when_to_use: EVM, Solidity tooling or blockchain clients that need exact 256-bit wrapping arithmetic; evmone already depends on it.
Hot loops over fixed 256- or 512-bit values where mpz allocation and size bookkeeping would dominate, e.g. small-operand division (256/64, 256/128) and full 256x256->512 products.
Code that needs compile-time (constexpr/consteval) big-integer constants, including division at compile time.
Projects that want a single header with no link dependency and can use C++20, on x86-64, arm64 or big-endian targets.
when_not_to_use: Operands that grow or vary in size (RSA, number theory, bignum factorials): there is no variable-size type, so use GMP, FLINT or Boost.Multiprecision.
You need a measured speedup over GMP before adopting: the repo has a GMP benchmark harness but publishes no results, so the claim is unproven (tier D).

Plain 128-bit math: a third-party harness (mikelik/int128-benchmark, 2023, GCC and Clang, 20-thread 4.6 GHz CPU) has intx::uint128 slower than unsigned __int128, absl::uint128 and even boost uint128_t for add (16.8 vs 1.74, 7.10, 13.2 ns with GCC); use the compiler builtin or _BitInt(128).
Repeated modular multiplication with a fixed modulus (elliptic-curve fields): mulmod computes the full product and then runs Knuth division, with no Montgomery or Barrett form.
Signed arithmetic as a type: there is no signed intN (issue #112 open); only sdivrem interprets the bits as two's complement.

integration.dependencies: none for the library (single include/intx/intx.hpp); the tests and intx-bench pull Google Benchmark via Hunter and need GMP
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (required since 0.10.0); CMake 3.16+ if using its CMake package; MSVC x64 19.44+ / arm64 19.50+ to avoid a compiler miscompile of addc in constant evaluation (issue #369)
integration.platforms: any 64-bit-word target; uses __int128 where available and _umul128 on MSVC x64, with portable fallbacks; CI covers non-x86 architectures and big-endian since 0.8.0; 32-bit Windows build fixed in 0.9.1
integration.thread_safety: Plain value types with no mutable global state (the only global is a constexpr reciprocal lookup table), so concurrent use of distinct objects is safe; not otherwise documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces fixed-size uses of GMP's mpn layer (the 64-bit words are layout-compatible, as the repo's own gmp.hpp wrappers cast them to mp_limb_t), but has no mpz/mpf API, no variable sizes and no signed type

gotchas: Division by zero is undefined behavior in release builds: INTX_REQUIRE is assert() with NDEBUG unset and __builtin_unreachable() otherwise.

from_string<uint256>() silently wraps some out-of-range 78-digit decimal inputs (issue #343, e.g. a value just above 2^256-1 parses as 9); the fix, PR #370, was still unmerged when checked, so validate untrusted decimal input yourself.
from_string/to_string throw std::invalid_argument or std::out_of_range; with -fno-exceptions they print to stderr and abort(). Arithmetic operators are noexcept.
Xcode 14.3.1 on arm64 miscompiled __builtin_subcll; intx works around it from 0.9.3 and 0.10.1 (CHANGELOG, PR #294), so older intx versions built with that Xcode can give wrong subtraction results.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick intx over ctbignum or Boost.Multiprecision's fixed cpp_int when you want a minimal, production-tested (evmone) uint256/uint512 value type with EVM helpers and byte-order I/O; pick ctbignum for fixed-modulus Montgomery arithmetic or Boost cpp_int when you need signed or checked types, since both publish measured wins over GMP and intx does not.
verified_claims_summary: Nothing has been measured against GMP in public: intx-bench registers uint256/uint512 udivrem against mpn_tdiv_qr and multiplication against mpn_mul_n (Google Benchmark, CMake Release, -falign-functions=32, no -march), but no results are committed or quoted. The only published numbers are intx versus earlier intx (PR #99: 256-bit division by 64- and 128-bit values up to 40% faster) and PR #367's CI medians across 13 CPU types, where intx's software reciprocal_2by1 is 2-3x slower than the x86 divq instruction on Ice Lake and Zen 5 (11.4 vs 4.0 ns; 8.9 vs 4.1 ns) but 4.7x faster on Coffee Lake (5.7 vs 26.4 ns).
status_note: Actively maintained by one maintainer (v0.15.0 released 2026-01-30; reciprocal benchmarks merged 2026-10-01), Apache-2.0, a single header that is easy to vendor, also on Conan Center.
